title: Advanced Instructions: HEALTHCHECK, ONBUILD & More 🧬
description: Explore less common but powerful Dockerfile instructions that make your images smarter.

slides.title: `HEALTHCHECK` – Container Self‑Diagnosis 🩺
slides.content:
# Tell Docker How to Check Health

By default, Docker only knows if a container’s main process is running. But a process can be alive yet unresponsive.

```dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK [OPTIONS] CMD <command>
```

**Options:**
- `--interval=DURATION` (default 30s)
- `--timeout=DURATION` (default 30s)
- `--start-period=DURATION` (initial grace time)
- `--retries=N` (default 3)

**Example:**
```dockerfile
HEALTHCHECK --interval=5s --timeout=3s CMD curl -f http://localhost/ || exit 1
```

Docker will run this command periodically. If it fails, the container’s status becomes `unhealthy`.

quizData.question: What happens when a container’s HEALTHCHECK command fails?

options.text: The container status changes to 'unhealthy' (and can be used by orchestrators)

quizData.explanation: Docker reports the status as unhealthy, but does not restart by itself unless a restart policy is also configured.

slides.title: `ONBUILD` – Triggers for Child Images 👶
slides.content:
# Instructions Deferred to Derived Images

`ONBUILD` stores a command that will be executed **only when this image is used as a base for another build**.

```dockerfile
ONBUILD INSTRUCTION
```

**Example:**
```dockerfile
ONBUILD COPY . /app
```

If you build `my-base` with this line, nothing happens. But when someone writes `FROM my-base`, the `COPY . /app` runs automatically in their build.

> Useful for framework base images (e.g., a Node.js base that copies package.json and runs npm install).

quizData.question: When does an `ONBUILD` instruction execute?

options.text: During the build of the image containing the ONBUILD
When the image is used as a base for another Dockerfile build
When a container is started from the image

quizData.explanation: ONBUILD defers the instruction to the next build that uses the image as a FROM line.

slides.title: `STOPSIGNAL` & `SHELL` ⚙️
slides.content:
# Fine‑Tuning Process Behaviour

- **STOPSIGNAL**: sets the system call signal that will be sent to the container to stop it (default is `SIGTERM`).
  ```dockerfile
  STOPSIGNAL SIGQUIT
  ```
- **SHELL**: changes the default shell used for the shell form of instructions.
  ```dockerfile
  SHELL ["/bin/bash", "-c"]
  RUN echo $HOME  # now uses bash
  ```
  Useful for images that don’t have `/bin/sh` or need a specific shell.

slides.title: `USER` – Running as Non‑Root 👤
slides.content:
# Security Best Practice

```dockerfile
USER <user>[:<group>]
# or
USER <UID>[:<GID>]
```

Changes the user for all subsequent `RUN`, `CMD`, `ENTRYPOINT`.

- Always create a dedicated user and switch to it before the final `CMD`.
- Example:
  ```dockerfile
  RUN addgroup -S appgroup && adduser -S appuser -G appgroup
  USER appuser
  ```
- Running as root inside a container is risky (especially if combined with `--privileged` or volume mounts).

quizData.question: By default, a Docker container runs as root unless the image specifies otherwise.
quizData.explanation: Unless the Dockerfile uses `USER`, the container process will run as root (UID 0).
